story.card_text: In the early hours of March 18, 1990, two men in police uniforms rang the museum's intercom, said they were responding to a disturbance, and were let in. They were inside 81 minutes. They left with thirteen works, among them Vermeer's The Concert, Rembrandt's Christ in the Storm on the Sea of Galilee - his only seascape - Manet's Chez Tortoni, five works by Degas, an ancient Chinese bronze beaker, and a bronze eagle finial. The Rembrandt was cut from its frame. None of it has come back. Isabella Stewart Gardner's will said the galleries were not to be permanently changed, so the empty frames still hang where the paintings were. The museum's reward for information leading to the works stands at $10 million, with a separate $100,000 for the eagle. The BPL's history put the haul at $200 million at the time. It is still unsolved. Outside, on the chimney over the old front door facing the Fens, is Gardner's carved crest: a phoenix rising from the ashes, and her motto, C'est mon plaisir - it's my pleasure.
story.headline: Thirteen works were taken from the Gardner in 1990, and the empty frames still hang where they were.

story.narration_script: Stand on The Fenway and look at the old front door with the two marble lions. In the early hours of March eighteenth, nineteen ninety, two men in police uniforms rang this museum's intercom, said they were answering a disturbance, and were let in. They stayed eighty-one minutes. They left with thirteen works, among them a Vermeer, a Rembrandt cut right out of its frame, a Manet, five Degas works, an ancient Chinese bronze, and a bronze eagle off a flagpole. None of it has come back. Isabella Stewart Gardner's will said the galleries weren't to be permanently changed, so the empty frames still hang where the paintings were. The reward for information stands at ten million dollars. It is still unsolved. Now look up at the chimney over the door. That's Gardner's crest: a phoenix rising out of the ashes, and her motto. It means, it's my pleasure.

finale.text: That's the walk: a jail called Liberty, a grasshopper, a mayor, a garage, a lieutenant governor's front door, a sloop, a gibbet, a price gouger's plaque, Kidd's cell, a stairway, a newspaper and a governor's door. Most of the people who made these scores got caught. The Brink's gang got life. Kidd got sixteen pounds of iron. Ponzi got his name on the thing, and Sarah Howe, who did it first, got three years and no credit. The ones who were never caught - the Gardner thieves, the crowd with axes on Garden Court - are still the best stories in town. Nobody's checked whether you took anything.

pitch_60: In the summer of nineteen twenty, the line for Charles Ponzi's office ran up a dark stairway on School Street and back around the block, and his clerks ran out of drawers for the cash. Forty years earlier, a fortune teller in the South End had already run the same scheme. Big Scores is a walk through three and a half centuries of Boston getting robbed, swindled and, now and then, catching the guy. The jail that held a mayor and is now a hotel. The door where Captain Kidd was arrested. The building the Brink's gang walked out of with a million dollars, and what it does for a living now. A pirate who retied his own noose. A crowd with axes at the lieutenant governor's front door. Every legend gets told, then checked against the court record. Every stop is a riddle, and every answer is something you read off a wall, a marker or a roof. It starts outside the old jail at Charles Street, on the Red Line. seo.landing_copy:
Boston likes to tell its history as a story about principle. This walk tells the other one: the money. Twelve stops from the old Charles Street Jail to the Province House site on Washington Street, plus a South End bonus stop and a detour to the Fens, covering three centuries of the city's biggest scores and best cons.

You'll start at the jail that held Boston's con artists, now a hotel called the Liberty. You'll stand outside the building where, on a January night in 1950, men in peacoats and Halloween masks took more than a million dollars in cash. You'll find the lot where Captain Kidd sat in irons in 1699, and the door he walked through when he was taken. You'll climb to the corner where Charles Ponzi's line formed in the summer of 1920, and walk a block to the street that took him down. You'll learn which famous Boston smuggler was never convicted of smuggling, which beloved mayor did time twice, which founding merchant was fined for gouging, and who ran Ponzi's scheme on Boston forty years before Ponzi.

Every stop is a riddle that walks you to the spot, and every answer is something you read on site - a date on a tablet, a number on a door - from the public sidewalk, day or night. Every story is sourced to court records, the FBI's own case files, governors' letters, a judge's diary and the papers of the day. Where a famous story doesn't hold up, we tell it and then show you the record.

About two and a half hours, about four kilometres, mostly flat. Short cuts for an hour in the North End or an hour downtown. Any two stops free; the whole walk is $1.99.

story.card_text: The gilded grasshopper on Faneuil Hall's cupola is about four feet of copper, and in the winter of 1973 to 1974 somebody took it. The New York Times put the theft between Christmas and January 4. The City's archives say it was gone for more than six months. The detective in charge was Paul Revere Carroll, a descendant of the man himself. It came back after the Plymouth County district attorney called him to say he had part of it. By Boston.com's account, the man who owned up was a steeplejack, someone who climbs buildings for a living, and he admitted it while facing drug charges and hoping for a better deal. He isn't named, and no court record of the theft has been published. The vane has had a locking device ever since. Shem Drowne, a coppersmith, made it for Peter Faneuil, copying the grasshopper on Sir Thomas Gresham's crest at London's Royal Exchange. The 1755 earthquake knocked it down and Drowne put it back up. As for the story that a Gresham baby was found in a field by a chirping grasshopper, the London Bullion Market Association calls it probably apocryphal.

story.card_text: In 1947, at 72 and in his fourth term as mayor, James Michael Curley lost his last appeal on a mail fraud conviction and told the Globe he would run the city from a cell. It wasn't his first time. In 1904, as a young alderman, he served time in the Charles Street Jail, where this walk started, for what Britannica calls 'impersonating a friend at a civil service examination' - he sat the test in someone else's place. The later case was over the Engineers Group, a wartime outfit that took deposits from businesses hoping for government contracts. The appeals court record puts the deposits at about $67,000, with about $9,600 paid back. He served five months of a six-month sentence in Danbury before President Truman commuted it, and Truman gave him a full pardon in 1950. The City Clerk, John Hynes, ran Boston while he was away, then beat him in 1949. The tablet here, put up in 1980, gives Curley the full resume: Congress twice, mayor of Boston four times, governor once, and Boston City Hospital as his monument. It leaves out both sentences.

The city clerk, John Hynes, ran Boston while he was gone, and two years later Hynes beat him. Now read the tablet. Congress twice, mayor four times, governor once. Nothing about either sentence.

He promised $150 back for every $100 in ninety days, and started paying in forty-five. story.card_text: In the summer of 1920 Charles Ponzi, still a hero to the crowds, walked past the Boston Post's office on this street shouting 'Three groans for the Post!' The paper was about to finish him. Washington Street from here north toward State Street was Newspaper Row: the Post, the Globe, the Herald, the Journal, the Advertiser and the Transcript all printed within a few blocks. In July 1920 the Post's publisher, Richard Grozier, became convinced Ponzi was a fraud. On Monday, July 26, the Post put the financier Clarence Barron's verdict on its front page - the reply coupons couldn't carry that kind of money - and the run on School Street began that day. On August 2 the Post ran a second exposé, and on August 11 it printed the story that finished him: a 'Charles Ponsi' had done time in Montreal. In 1921 the Post won the Pulitzer Prize for Public Service, 'for its exposure of the operations of Charles Ponzi by a series of articles which finally led to his arrest.' The Post's own 1874 building is right next door, lettered for Franklin's birthplace; by 1920 the paper had moved up Washington Street, to a building since torn down. These two buildings are, by the National Register's count, all that's left of the row.

story.card_text: On Thursday, July 6, 1699, Captain William Kidd came in by the door of the governor's lodging here and, in the governor's own words, 'rushed in and came running to me, the Constable after him.' He was seized. Kidd, wanted for piracy, had come to Boston that summer to deal with the Earl of Bellomont, who was living in Peter Sergeant's house on this spot; Sergeant had been talked into moving across the street. The house was built in 1679 and bought by the Province in 1716 as the governors' residence. Kidd went to the jail on Court Street. A committee searched his lodgings and found gold and silver 'hid and made up in two seabeds,' including 'a bag of gold dust and ingots of the value of about £1,000.' Now the legend: Kidd's treasure, buried on some island and never found. The record: he had left a parcel with Mr. Gardiner of Gardiner's Island, and Gardiner handed it over, worth perhaps £4,500, Bellomont reckoned. By July 25 the inventory of everything held from Kidd listed 1,111 ounces of gold and 2,353 of silver. Kidd was shipped to London and hanged in 1701.

story.card_text: Forty years before Ponzi, there was Sarah Howe. Around 1879 she opened the Ladies' Deposit in the South End. It took money only from single women who didn't own real estate, between $200 and $1,000 a deposit, and paid eight percent a month, three months in advance. She said Quakers were behind it, out of charity for unprotected women. The Atlantic Monthly later said she had 'no more hold upon the Quakers than she had upon the Pope.' Somewhere over a thousand women signed up. Howe bought a house on this square, across from the St. James Hotel, reportedly worth $40,000. In September 1880 the Boston Daily Advertiser ran 'A Mysterious Bank,' the run started, and in mid-October she was arrested and committed to the Charles Street Jail, where this walk started. In April 1881 she was sentenced to three years on four counts of cheating by false pretenses. Out in 1884, she opened the Woman's Bank on Concord Street at seven percent a month. It collapsed in 1887. The legend says Ponzi invented the Ponzi scheme. He didn't even invent it in Boston.

story.narration_script: Forty years before Ponzi, there was Sarah Howe. Around eighteen seventy-nine she opened the Ladies' Deposit in the South End. It only took money from single women who didn't own property, and it paid eight percent a month, three months up front. She said Quakers were behind it, out of charity. A magazine later said she had no more hold on the Quakers than she had on the Pope. More than a thousand women signed up. Howe bought a house on this square, across from the old St. James Hotel. In September of eighteen eighty, a Boston paper ran a story called A Mysterious Bank. The run started, and in October she was arrested and sent to the Charles Street Jail. She got three years for cheating by false pretenses. When she got out, she opened the Woman's Bank on Concord Street at seven percent a month. That one collapsed too. The legend says Ponzi invented the Ponzi scheme. He didn't even invent it in Boston.

web.teaser: Forty years before Ponzi, a former fortune teller named Sarah Howe ran a bank in the South End for single women only, at eight percent a month. Over a thousand women signed up. She bought a house on a fenced green square across from a grand hotel, and in 1881 she got three years. The square and the hotel building are both still there. Take the Silver Line.

summary: Three and a half centuries of Boston getting robbed, swindled and, now and then, catching the guy: the jail that held the con artists, the Brink's job, the door Captain Kidd was arrested at, the stairway where Ponzi took in nine and a half million dollars, the wharf where Hancock lost a sloop and kept his record, and the woman who ran the Ponzi scheme forty years before Ponzi. Every legend gets told, then checked against the court record.
